Title: Chief Operating Officer
Talk Track: I ran platform and reliability engineering at Tricentis, a software-testing company, after leading QA automation and developer platforms at PayPal and Ripple — my whole career has been moving release quality out of people's hands and into systems. Your VP of Engineering posting asks for someone who has "personally rescued or rebuilt automation programs in multi-platform environments" and can shift the org from "manual-heavy to automation-first," and it says the role leads a QA organization of eight manual QA engineers and two automation QA engineers across eight value streams. The number to read there is the ratio, not the title: with quality capacity that manual, each new value stream adds QA headcount instead of amortizing it, so cost-to-deliver climbs in step with the client count you keep announcing. The instinct is to hire more automation engineers; the cheaper first move is release gates plus a test-data and environment-parity layer, so the ten people you already have produce automation as a byproduct of the work they do anyway. That reorders the hiring plan rather than enlarging it, which is worth knowing whether or not you ever talk to me. Is the ratio something you have already priced in? — Daniel Kirichanski, Prime Path Global

Title: Co-founder
Talk Track: I spent the last year at Tricentis putting AI agents into production for incident detection and on-call response, and before that ran platform engineering at Ripple and PayPal - the work was always making cost-to-deliver stop scaling one-for-one with headcount. Your Applied AI Lead posting asks one person to both "identify where AI can eliminate manual work, reduce cycle time" and "serve as the technical guardrail for AI work happening across the company." Read against the same posting's line about being "at an inflection point," the number that quietly decides the next round is cost-to-serve per MSP staying flat while AP and analytics revenue grows. Is the guardrail layer getting designed before or after the first agents ship? - Daniel Kirichanski, Prime Path Global

Why This Company (signal): Unlock Health is a PE-backed healthcare marketing roll-up (Eruptr + DECODE + SPM Group) whose live Head of Web Engineering posting asks one hire to both 'drive profitability, optimizing utilization' of the web development practice and 'champion responsible and performant AI development practices, including robust CI/CD pipelines that support increased development velocity' - a headcount-bound, high-touch delivery org publicly confessing Daniel's exact EDP, that cost-to-deliver must stop scaling one-for-one with headcount.
Title: Vice President, Finance
Talk Track: Most of my last decade went into making delivery stop scaling one-for-one with headcount - PayPal's CI/CD platform for 9,000+ developers, Ripple's deploy cycles from hours down to minutes, and AI agents at Tricentis that took MTTR down roughly 40%. Your Head of Web Engineering posting on Greenhouse asks one hire to 'operate as the business leader of the web development discipline with a focus on driving profitability, optimizing utilization,' and in that same list to 'champion responsible and performant AI development practices, including robust CI/CD pipelines that support increased development velocity.' Read together, that is a margin problem wearing an engineering job description. Utilization is a ceiling rather than a lever - a practice can only bill the hours it staffs, so profitability actually moves when the delivery pipeline raises output per engineer, not when someone resources projects more thoughtfully. The part that usually bites: an AI-native leader dropped onto a practice that has no delivery platform underneath it just adds review load onto the same tech leads, and velocity goes flat around month four. Where does the web practice sit on output per engineer today? - Daniel Kirichanski, Prime Path Global

Title: Head of Product
Talk Track: I ran platform engineering at Ripple through 6B+ annual transactions, and PayPal's internal developer platform for 9,000 engineers before that, so I've watched what happens when corridors grow faster than the engineering underneath them. Your Product Manager, Onboarding posting puts it plainly: "We have built a world-class financial engine. Now we need an onboarding experience that matches it." Read alongside the Developer Experience Lead req — "how external developers experience that engine has no owner" — those two openings are describing one number rather than two: how many OpenFX people it takes to get one institution live and trading. At $45B annualized across 100+ institutional clients, that number decides whether each new corridor compounds margin or just adds a delivery team. In my experience that is almost always solved with plumbing — a self-serve integration path, API governance, docs that stay true as the platform moves — and only rarely with more headcount. What does it cost you today to get one institution to first trade?

Stage: Growth-stage, PE- and debt-backed; ~207 employees (41 technical); $195.5M total funding across 6 rounds (private equity round 2017; debt led by Pollen Street Capital 2019, Forbright Bank 2022); founded 2014
Why This Company (signal): Koalafi has two live platform-engineering leadership postings (Engineering Lead, Platform Engineering and Lead Platform Engineer, both reposted) whose JD asks the hire to 'design and implement automation and self-service workflows using infrastructure-as-code, APIs, and developer platforms to reduce developer friction' while a Cloud Architect already owns platform strategy - the exact strategy-to-delivery platform gap Daniel closed at PayPal (CI/CD platform for 9,000+ developers) and Ripple (deploys hours to minutes), in his deepest vertical, payments/fintech.
Title: Chief Operating Officer
Talk Track: Charles - I ran platform engineering at Ripple and PayPal, where the work was turning architecture standards into a developer platform people actually shipped on: deploy cycles went from hours to minutes, and at PayPal that platform served 9,000+ developers. Your Lead Platform Engineer posting asks the hire to 'design and implement automation and self-service workflows using infrastructure-as-code, APIs, and developer platforms to reduce developer friction,' working alongside a Cloud Architect who already owns platform strategy and standards. Read plainly, that is a strategy-to-delivery gap rather than a headcount gap - the standards are written, and nobody has the capacity to make them the default path engineers take. Built In shows the two versions of that role reposted at 15 and 22 days, which is what usually happens when you are hiring for the translation layer between architecture and delivery; that market is thin. Meanwhile the same JD asks the hire to champion AI-assisted development, which lands on pipelines that have to verify what gets generated - verification capacity, not more implementers, is what makes that safe. What has the platform team not shipped this quarter?
